Some considerations.

Not everything can or will even if it can be automated. Future jobs that benefit from human empathy and touch will grow. Health care is a good example.

Also, long life spans will mean both lower labor force participation and more intensive personal services for old farts who stop mowing the lawn, doing repairs around the house, cooking meals, cleaning pools and start needing hip replacements, rehab after puling a back muscle etc. etc.

Further, new jobs will likely be created in places that we cannot imagine today. Think of all of the jobs of today that we did not have in the past.

Automation increases productivity and productivity is one of the key components for increasing prosperity.

There are legitimate concerns about the winners and losers under future developments, the impacts on society in general and on those specific individuals who get left behind or fall somewhere lower on the economic scale as a result. This is a legitimate area for public policy to consider how best to address. Do nothing and let happen happen? Basic income? Minimum Wage? Earned Income Tax Credits? etc. etc.

I believe the best solutions will be those that are balanced and moderate in nature and that recognize both the desirability to maintain a strong economy that continues to advance in areas such as automation but that also is sensitive to a responsibility to ensure people are not diminished in the process.

Perhaps a rational for basic income may come into play some day. No one would have believed the Central Bank could print $4 trillion in dollar bills without creating hyperinflation and yet it could and did because of the tremendous imbalance in supply and demand. Maybe this is a harbinger of economic conditions to come whereby the incomes of workers no longer are adequate to generate economic demand and the wealth of owners is too concentrated to offset. Hence a basic income funded out of thin air might become a new reality as absurd as this may have sounded just 5 years ago?

But this is far too soon to tell and to enact basic income today could also have disastrous long term consequences on work ethics, cultures, self reliance, ability to move away from subsistence levels, etc.

What we can do today is: 1) raise the cutoff for salaries as Obama is doing

2) moderately increase the minimum wage in order to place upward pressure on wage scales but not so high as to significantly lock out groups from the labor market,

3) Adjust the minimum wage in local markets to partially reflect costs of living. It is absurd to have the same minimum wage in West Virginia as in New York City or San Francisco.

4) moderately increase benefits under the earned income tax credit program to target assistance to working poor families and achieve a living wage without disrupting the markets as would a $15 minimum wage.

5) Provide a taxpayer financed health care system for the poor to remove this burden from employers and shift it to the personal income tax through progressive rates.

These are some of the labor force actions that could be pursued in a moderate, measured and balanced fashion. Of course there are a whole host of other actions to spur economic growth , fix corporate tax rates, re establish a level playing field for economic growth, encourage new start up businesses, reduce crony corporate capitalism and government corruption and eliminate circumstances where TBTF banks can blackmail and hold hostage the nation.
